name: The Everyday Go-To
why: The periwinkle tee is one of your three swatch-test-validated colours; the seafoam chino tested as the flattest of six swatches (§Phase 3.4), so it's carried here by the top, not doing work itself. Corrected: dropped the 'work' tag — a heavyweight tee is formality 'casual', below the business-casual floor this role actually needs (Phase 1: client-facing daily, leadership-visible almost daily), and tee+jogger/chino is explicitly the pre-roadmap habit this whole project exists to move past, not a validated office look.

name: Neutral Reset
why: White + dark olive reads clean, no clash risk. Swapped off seafoam — the pairings audit found it carrying 7 different looks, out of proportion to how many trousers actually exist (§Phase 4). Dropped the 'work' tag for the same reason as The Everyday Go-To — plain tee tops cap the outfit at Casual formality, not business-casual.

name: Statement Bottom
why: Salmon carries the outfit — keep the top neutral.

name: Clean Base, Earth Bottom
why: Corrected: the heavyweight tee is Relaxed Fit (verified against Zara's own listing), same volume class as the jogger — two loose pieces together reads sloppy at 172cm. jj-tee-white's regular fit is the only owned casual top that can balance relaxed loungewear correctly.

name: Utility Contrast
why: Corrected: previously paired a Relaxed-fit tee with baggy cargo — both loose, the exact combo the cargo's own note warns against. White regular-fit top now carries the contrast instead of a tonal grey-to-black match.

name: Activate the Woodland
why: Corrected: swapped the relaxed jogger for the regular-fit khaki denim so the relaxed tee has a fitted counterpoint — still rugged-casual, still finally gives the boot an outfit, and gives the previously-unpaired khaki denim its first look too.

name: Forest, Earth Base
why: Replaces the old 'Purple + Black' pairing, which relied on a Relaxed tee + baggy cargo combo that no longer passes proportion rules. Dark green (relaxed) needs a fitted/regular bottom, not another loose one — khaki denim fits and was otherwise sitting with zero outfits of its own.

name: The One Smart Option (today)
why: As close to business-casual as the current wardrobe gets — kept tagged 'work' as the one usable stopgap before the 30-day MTM shirts land, but the tee still caps this at Casual formality, not genuine business-casual. Swapped seafoam for the charcoal trouser once it exists — a pastel chino under a Derby+belt combo undercut the whole point of this look; charcoal actually earns the 'smart' in the name. Treat it as a bridge, not a destination.

name: Statement Shirt, Plain Base
why: The one patterned piece already owned — its own note says pair with plain neutral bottoms only, since the stripe is already doing the work. Gives it its first complete look.

name: Client Day
why: 60/30/10 — navy, white, tan/steel accent.

name: Daily Elevated
why: One of your three swatch-test-validated near-face colours, plus tan — also validated (§Phase 3.4) — at the shoe. Swapped chino-navy for the charcoal trouser to give the ₹4,730 tailored piece an actual outfit — it was sitting on one look while navy carried six.

name: AC-Swing Fix
why: Tonal navy column + decoupled indoor layer.

name: Sky Blue Basics
why: Classic office pairing, no jacket needed.

name: Charcoal Everything
why: Single neutral, zero clash risk.

name: Weekend Denim
why: Reads fine with tan or black belt. Note: since jeans-dark moved to a BSC black stretch jean (§Phase 4, vendor consolidation), this is closer to a dark trouser than true rigid denim — still works the same way in an outfit, just flagged for accuracy.

name: Stone Bridge
why: Bridges old earth-tone habits with the new palette.

name: Wine Layer, Cool Evening
why: Warmer register, casual enough for the knit. Swapped chino-navy for the black jean — navy was carrying six looks already, and a business-casual chino under a knit crew reads more mismatched than a jean does here.

name: Flight Day
why: Corrected, two fixes: the overshirt is relaxed and so, now correctly, is the heavyweight tee — stacking two loose pieces reads sloppy, so the regular-fit jj-tee-white goes underneath instead. Also swapped chino-navy for jeans-dark, since business-casual chino paired with an athletic sneaker was too wide a formality gap to read as deliberate.

name: Monsoon Commute
why: Corrected: the original business shirt + chino + athletic sneaker combo was too wide a formality gap (and impractical — leather dress shoes don't belong in monsoon rain anyway). Elevated-casual polo + dark jeans is the realistic register for a rainy commute in sneakers, shell over the top for the AC/rain swing.

name: Abroad, Off-Duty
why: Low-maintenance, no ironing needed on the road.

name: Festive Register
why: Separate formality register — not Western business-casual at all.

name: Navy Shirt, Charcoal Base
why: The 30-day navy MTM shirt had zero outfits built around it. Swapped seafoam for the charcoal trouser — this is a genuine business-casual register, and a pastel chino was undercutting it the same way it did in 'The One Smart Option'.

name: First Pattern, Kept Low-Risk
why: The houndstooth stays subtle because everything below it is solid navy and tan — deliberately restrained per the roadmap's own reasoning for adding this shirt.

name: Second Register, Work
why: The Cocoleni Hermann Honey gives work days a second visual register, distinct from the Zweig's rounded everyday softness — and its honey/amber tone is itself swatch-test-validated (§Phase 3.4). Swapped chino-navy for the charcoal trouser, which was underused relative to how often navy repeats elsewhere.

name: Gym Session
why: The only fully athletic-register look in the wardrobe — pre-empting the incoming gym habit.

name: Abroad, Off-Duty (Sun)
why: Same low-maintenance travel base as the Zweig version, swapped for sunglasses when it's actually sunny out.

name: Olive on Khaki
why: Restores the olive tee's outfit after the Relaxed-fit correction moved it off the (also relaxed) cream jogger — tonal earth column, now with a regular-fit bottom instead of a second loose piece.

name: Olive Trouser, Cognac Anchor
why: The 18-month olive chino paired with the swatch-test-validated cognac Derby and belt — a second real neutral-adjacent trouser besides charcoal and navy, built specifically so the two cognac pieces have more than one bottom to anchor.

name: Linen Shirt, Charcoal Base
why: The 18-month linen shirt is the first fabric change from Washed Oxford — built on the charcoal trouser rather than another navy pairing, since by this point charcoal has earned regular rotation, not a one-off.

name: Tiger on Black
why: Black cargo picks up the shoe's own black stripes and suede toe, the white regular-fit tee gives the baggy cargo its fitted counterpoint (the same correction already applied to Utility Contrast), and the yellow is the lone accent against two neutrals — 60/30/10 with the 10% on the feet. Streetwear register, the closest this wardrobe gets to the casual-layering reference named in Phase 1. Correction to the first version of this note: it claimed this was the only clean home the shoe had in the owned wardrobe, reasoning that the seafoam chino was a muted colour. That was wrong — it took seafoam's hex from palette.json's swatch-test record (#B9D4C4) rather than the #9DC9B0 in items.json that the classifier actually reads, and at that value seafoam is a saturated accent, not a muted one. The owned wardrobe passes 19 combinations with this shoe, not one. See White, Navy, Yellow and Retro on Retro for the two others worth curating.

name: Grey Base, Tiger Accent
why: The travel version of Abroad, Off-Duty, with the Tiger doing the colour work instead of the Cloudtilt keeping everything quiet. Grey tee and black jean both classify as true neutrals, so the yellow is the only accent and reads deliberate rather than accidental; relaxed tee over slim jean supplies the fitted counterpoint. Needs the black jeans off the roadmap — which is the strongest practical argument for buying them, since they roughly double the number of places this shoe can go.

name: Charcoal Polo, Tiger Accent
why: Elevated weekend — the 2-3x/month "nice place" dinners from Phase 1. Charcoal polo and black jean are both neutral, so the shoe stays the single accent even though the outfit sits a full formality tier above the cargo look. This is the pairing where the Japan polo buy and the shoe pay for each other: charcoal is the one new top that lifts the Tiger's register without competing with it for attention.

name: The Tiger's Ceiling
why: The dressiest this shoe goes, and deliberately not tagged for work: Phase 1 recorded client-facing contact as daily and leadership visibility as near-daily, and a bright yellow sneaker doesn't clear that floor however carefully it's styled — the same reasoning that pulled the 'work' tag off The Everyday Go-To and Neutral Reset. Keep it for a no-meetings day or straight after one. Note the colour arithmetic: navy classifies as a saturated accent in this system rather than a neutral, so navy chino plus yellow shoe is already a two-colour outfit and the polo has to stay neutral — swapping in the navy polo would push it to three and trip the ceiling.

name: White, Navy, Yellow
why: The best thing the Tiger does with pieces already owned, and the look the first pass missed. Navy and yellow are complementary, which §Phase 3's harmony rules allow only when one dominates and never 50/50 — here the navy chino is most of the outfit and the shoe is the accent, so it lands on the right side of that line. White tee keeps the count at two colours. The navy chino is slim and the tee is regular, so the proportion reads clean at 172cm. Wearable today with nothing bought.

name: Retro on Retro
why: A 1966 running silhouette under a retro striped shirt — the two owned pieces with actual period character, used together on purpose. The black-and-off-white stripe classifies as neutral, so the colour count stays at navy plus yellow; the stripe is doing pattern work, not colour work. Relaxed shirt over the slim navy chino gives the fitted counterpoint. This is the one Tiger look that would survive a nice dinner rather than just a cafe.

name: Errand Run
why: The red Skechers had no curated look at all until now, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight: it is the only owned shoe at formality 'athletic', which hard-conflicts with every business-casual bottom, and its red is a saturated accent that blows the 3-colour ceiling the moment any coloured top or muted bottom joins it. Run the whole owned wardrobe against it and exactly four combinations pass clean — all four are this white regular-fit tee over a relaxed jogger or the black cargo, because every relaxed Zara tee conflicts with every relaxed jogger on volume. This is that look at its most honest: a cushioned slip-on, a jogger, a white tee, red as the single accent. Athleisure, and not pretending otherwise.

name: Walking Day
why: Deliberately the same top and bottom as Tiger on Black, with the shoe swapped — because the two shoes are not interchangeable on a long day out. The Mexico 66 is a flat leather sole over a thin insole; it is the better-looking shoe and the wrong one for twenty thousand steps around a city. The Ultra Flex is a cushioned slip-on, which is precisely what it is good for. Same neutral base, red instead of yellow as the single accent. Keep this pair in mind as a swap rather than two separate outfits.

name: Wine on Navy
why: Burgundy over navy is one of the oldest safe pairs in menswear and it needs nothing bought but the polo — the chino and the sneakers are already owned. Two saturated accents, which the 2026-08-30 swatch test validated regardless of warm/cool mix, and the white sneaker keeps the base quiet. Clears the business-casual floor for a normal office day: polo at elevated-casual, chino at business-casual, one tier apart.

name: Daily Elevated, Wine
why: The buildable twin of Daily Elevated. That look is the flagship of the daily elevated-casual register and it is built on the emerald polo — which, after the 2026-10-25 Uniqlo Japan check, has no identified product behind it at any brand. This is the same outfit in a colour that can actually be bought, in the same week, for ¥2,990. Wine and tan are the two accents against the charcoal; emerald stays on the roadmap as the aspiration rather than the only path to this register.

name: Wine, Black, Off-Duty
why: Gives the wine polo a casual home as well as a work one, so it isn't a single-register buy. Black cargo and white sneaker are both neutral, leaving the wine as the only accent — the same 60/30/10 structure as the Tiger looks, with the colour moved from the feet to the face, which is where the swatch test says a saturated colour actually earns its keep. Note this is the one wine look that works with the baggy cargo: the polo's regular fit is the fitted counterpoint.

name: Navy Polo, Charcoal Base
why: The navy polo's two existing looks both lean on outerwear — the overshirt for the AC swing, the shell for monsoon. This is the plain version underneath, which is what it will actually be worn as most days. Navy and tan are the accents, charcoal carries the 60%.

name: Stone, Navy, Tan
why: The stone polo passed 34 combinations and was curated into exactly one, which under-uses the most flexible top on the roadmap — it classifies as a true neutral, so it never counts toward the 3-colour ceiling and can sit under anything. Here it lets the navy chino and tan loafers be the two accents, which no other top in the plan does as cleanly.

name: Nothing to Decide
why: Scores All Neutral — zero accents, the safest combination the engine will return. Deliberately included: Phase 1 recorded a risk-averse buying pattern and a daily uniform worn because it was easy rather than considered, so the roadmap needs at least one business-casual look that requires no colour judgment at all on a morning with none to spare. The Seiko adds to it without changing the score, since a white dial reads neutral too.

name: Rest Day
why: The white jogger had no look at all. Nor did the khaki or the olive — all three are colourways of one garment, and the engine gives each of them the same three clean options, because every relaxed Zara tee conflicts with every relaxed jogger on volume and the J&J regular-fit tee is the only owned casual top left standing. Rather than three interchangeable entries, each jogger gets a different shoe and a different job. This is the white one with the cushioned Skechers: the most comfortable combination in the wardrobe and the least styled, which is the honest description of a day at home.

name: Weekend Errand, Earth
why: The khaki jogger's look, and the Woodland boot's second — it had been carrying exactly one since the wardrobe audit, despite passing 29 combinations, because Phase 1 recorded it as unused for want of knowing what it goes with rather than dislike. Khaki and camel are both warm earth tones one step apart, which is analogous harmony, the safest scheme in §Phase 3's list. White tee keeps it from going muddy.

name: Olive Jogger, Quiet Shoe
why: The olive jogger's only clean combination in the entire owned wardrobe — one, against three for the white and khaki, because olive classifies as a muted accent and every other owned shoe turns it into a muted-plus-saturated pair. The ivory Cloudtilt is the one that stays neutral and lets it alone. Worth knowing before buying any more olive: below the waist it is fine, which §Phase 3's face rule already allows, but it earns less than the khaki does.

name: Stripe, Charcoal, Tan
why: The 24-month striped shirt was the last orphan on the roadmap. It is the second patterned business-casual piece after the houndstooth check, and the plan deliberately puts it last — by then the base is established, so a bolder register costs less risk. Charcoal trouser and tan leather, the same frame as every other shirt look here: the pattern is the only thing doing anything new, which is the whole point of introducing it late.

name: Salmon, Forest, White
why: The salmon chino passed 148 combinations — 52 of them entirely from owned pieces — and was curated into one. That is the widest coverage gap in the wardrobe. The dark green tee, also on one look, is the pairing that costs nothing: it measures as a neutral (s=0.175, just under the line), so the salmon is the single accent and the top does the quiet work. Both pieces were under-used for the same reason — neither had an obvious partner written down.

name: Periwinkle on Navy
why: The periwinkle tee is flagged a favourite and is one of only three swatch-test-validated near-face colours, yet it had a single look — The Everyday Go-To, which pairs it with the seafoam chino. This is the better version: periwinkle over navy is analogous (both blue-violet family, one deep and one mid), which §Phase 3 lists as a safe scheme, where periwinkle-over-seafoam is blue-violet against green and only works because the top carries it. Same two pieces of effort, stronger result.
